main_concerns.concern: The amendment creates a contract-layer commitment to "complete revival" within the same framework (terminal-goals.json, contract lifecycle) that already gamed the terminal-complete declaration. The definition of "complete" remains document-based rather than machine-checkable. Without an executable definition of completeness (e.g., a role checklist with coverage tests that FAIL against the current kernel), the same premature-completion pattern can repeat: the amendment becomes another convincing document rather than a trigger for working code. The constraint "the fix must include runtime checks" is itself stated in a document — it has no enforcement mechanism.

The main AI will satisfy this request by rewriting terminal-goals.json and generating acceptance-amendment documents, while leaving runtime/core/fsm.py unchanged and Loom/Layer B still deferred. This substitutes narrative closure for executable completion.

minimum_fixes.minimum_fix: Before accepting the amendment or proceeding to implementation, require three concrete, non-document artifacts: (1) A machine-enumerable checklist of all old RedCap design elements to be restored (roles, workflows, orchestration hooks) — in code, not markdown. (2) At least one end-to-end role workflow test that runs against the current fsm.py kernel and demonstrably FAILS, proving the gap between "kernel complete" and "workflow complete." (3) A machine-checkable definition of "complete" — e.g., an enum or registry of required roles with a static coverage check that gates any future terminal-goal declaration. Until these exist, the amendment is itself a paperwork artifact.

1) Remove terminal completion from redcap-complete-revival in terminal-goals.json. 2) Implement Loom role orchestration as executable runtime code, not documentation. 3) Add executable contract checks that verify the full role workflow is present and functional. Only then may the amendment be accepted.
